definition: Voltage (production), current, and load (demand) on a power system are physically linked; a grid stays stable only when generation is kept matched to demand.
core_idea: Because grid operators cannot directly throttle how much electricity consumers use, they must continuously adjust production to track demand. Too little generation causes brownouts; too much overloads transmission wires, which heat up and can melt, causing a blackout.
key_points: Excess current heats transmission wires; enough heat causes the wire to melt
Grid operators balance the system by adjusting supply, not demand, since demand isn't directly controllable
Undergeneration relative to demand causes brownouts
Overgeneration relative to demand can overheat lines and cause blackouts
relationships: Brownouts and blackouts are opposite failure modes of the same generation/demand mismatch problem
trading_implications: Explains the physical necessity of real-time balancing and frequency-responsive dispatch in power markets
caveats: Blackouts aren't only caused by too little power — producing too much relative to demand can also force an outage by melting lines
